source_text: Ἐπειδὰν γὰρ ἡ χάρις ἐλθοῦσα τὸ σκότος ἀπελάσῃ τῆς διανοίας, μανθάνομεν τὴν τῶν πραγμάτων ἀκρίβειαν, καὶ γίνεται ἡμῖν εὐκαταφρόνητα τὰ πρότερον φοβερά. Οὔτε γὰρ θάνατον ἔτι δεδοίκαμεν, μαθόντες ἀκριβῶς παρὰ τῆς ἱερᾶς ταύτης μυσταγωγίας, ὅτι οὐκ ἔστι θάνατος ὁ θάνατος, ἀλλ' ὕπνος καὶ κοίμησις πρόσκαιρος· οὐ πενίαν, οὐ νόσον, οὐκ ἄλλο τι τῶν τοιούτων οὐδὲν, εἰδότες ὅτι πρὸς βελτίονα ζωὴν ὁδεύομεν, ἀκήρατόν τε καὶ ἄφθαρτον, καὶ πάσης τοιαύτης ἀπηλλαγμένην ἀνωμαλίας. βʹ. Μὴ τοίνυν ἔτι πρὸς τὰ βιωτικὰ μείνωμεν κεχηνότες, μὴ περὶ τρυφὴν τραπέζης, μηδὲ περὶ πολυτέλειαν ἱματίων· καὶ γὰρ ἔχεις ἱμάτιον μέγιστον, ἔχεις τράπεζαν πνευματικὴν, ἔχεις τὴν δόξαν τὴν ἄνω, καὶ πάντα σοι ὁ Χριστὸς γίνεται, καὶ τράπεζα, καὶ ἱμάτιον, καὶ οἶκος, καὶ κεφαλὴ, καὶ ῥίζα. Ὅσοι γὰρ εἰς Χριστὸν ἐβαπτίσθητε, Χριστὸν ἐνεδύσασθε· ἰδοὺ πῶς ἱμάτιόν σοι γέγονε. Βούλει μαθεῖν, πῶς καὶ τράπεζά σοι γίνεται; Ὁ τρώγων με, φησὶν, ὥσπερ ἐγὼ ζῶ διὰ τὸν Πατέρα, κἀκεῖνος ζήσεται δι' ἐμέ. Ὅτι δὲ καὶ οἶκός σοι γίνεται· Ὁ τρώγων μου τὴν σάρκα ἐν ἐμοὶ μένει, κἀγὼ ἐν αὐτῷ· καὶ ὅτι ῥίζα, πάλιν φησίν· Ἐγὼ ἡ ἄμπελος, ὑμεῖς τὰ κλήματα· καὶ ὅτι ἀδελφὸς, καὶ φίλος, καὶ νυμφίος· Οὐκέτι ὑμᾶς λέγω δούλους· ὑμεῖς γὰρ φίλοι μου ἐστέ. Καὶ ὁ Παῦλος πάλιν· Ἡρμοσάμην ὑμᾶς ἑνὶ ἀνδρὶ παρθένον ἁγνὴν παραστῆσαι τῷ Χριστῷ· καὶ πάλιν· Εἰς τὸ εἶναι αὐτὸν πρωτότοκον ἐν πολλοῖς ἀδελφοῖς. Οὐκ ἀδελφοὶ δὲ αὐτοῦ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ παιδία γινόμεθα· Ἰδοὺ γὰρ, φησὶν, ἐγὼ, καὶ τὰ παιδία, ἅ μοι ἔδωκεν ὁ Θεός· οὐ τοῦτο δὲ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ μέλη αὐτοῦ, καὶ σῶμα αὐτοῦ. Ὥσπερ γὰρ οὐκ ἀρκούντων τῶν εἰρημένων ἐπιδεῖξαι τὴν ἀγάπην καὶ τὴν εὔνοιαν, ἣν πρὸς ἡμᾶς ἐπιδείκνυται, καὶ ἕτερον τούτων μεῖζον καὶ ἐγγύτερον ἔθηκεν, κεφαλὴν ἑαυτὸν ἡμῶν προσειπών. Ταῦτα δὴ πάντα εἰδὼς, ἀγαπητὲ, ἄμειψαί σου τὸν εὐεργέτην ἀρίστῃ πολιτείᾳ, καὶ ἐννοήσας τῆς θυσίας τὸ μέγεθος, καλλώπισόν σου τὰ μέλη τοῦ σώματος. Ἐννόησον τί δέχῃ τῇ χειρὶ, καὶ μηδέποτε ἀνάσχῃ τυπτῆσαί τινα, μηδὲ τὴν τοσούτῳ τιμηθεῖσαν δώρῳ καταισχύνῃς τῇ τῆς πληγῆς ἁμαρτίᾳ· ἐννόησον τί δέχῃ τῇ χειρὶ, καὶ καθαρὰν αὐτὴν πλεονεξίας καὶ ἁρπαγῆς πάσης διατήρησον. Λόγισαι, ὅτι οὐ τῇ χειρὶ δέχῃ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῷ στόματι προσάγεις καὶ καθαρὰν φύλαττε τὴν γλῶτ49.234 ταν αἰσχρῶν καὶ ὑβριστικῶν ῥημάτων, βλασφημίας, ἐπιορκίας, καὶ τῶν ἄλλων τῶν τοιούτων ἁπάντων. Καὶ γὰρ ὀλέθριον τὴν διακονουμένην μυστηρίοις οὕτω φρικωδεστάτοις, καὶ αἵματι φοινιχθεῖσαν τοιούτῳ, καὶ χρυσῆν γενομένην μάχαιραν, ἐπὶ λοιδορίας καὶ ὕβρεις καὶ εὐτραπελίας μετάγειν. Αἰδέσθητι τὴν τιμὴν, ἢν ἐτίμησεν αὐτὴν ὁ Θεὸς, καὶ μὴ καταγάγῃς εἰς τὴν τῆς ἁμαρτίας εὐτέλειαν· ἀλλ' ἐνθυμηθεὶς πάλιν, ὅτι μετὰ τὴν χεῖρα καὶ τὴν γλῶσσαν ἡ καρδία δέχεται τὸ φρικτὸν ἐκεῖνο μυστήριον, μὴ ῥάψῃς ποτὲ κατὰ τοῦ πλησίον δόλον, ἀλλὰ κακουργίας πάσης καθαρὰν διατήρει σου τὴν διάνοιαν· οὕτω καὶ ὀφθαλμοὺς καὶ ἀκοὴν ἀσφαλίσασθαι δυνήσῃ. Πῶς γὰρ οὐκ ἄτοπον, μετὰ τὴν μυστικὴν ἐκείνην φωνὴν καὶ ἐκ τῶν οὐρανῶν φερομένην, τὴν ἐκ τῶν Χερουβὶμ λέγω, πορνικοῖς ᾄσμασι καὶ κατακεκλασμένοις μέλεσι τὴν ἀκοὴν μολύνειν; πῶς δὲ οὐκ ἐσχάτης κολάσεως ἄξιον, τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς, οἷς ὁρᾷς τὰ ἀπόῤῥητα καὶ φρικτὰ μυστήρια, τούτοις πόρνας ὁρᾷν, καὶ μοιχείαν ἐργάζεσθαι τὴν κατὰ διάνοιαν; Εἰς γάμον ἐκλήθης, ἀγαπητέ· μὴ εἰσέλθῃς ῥυπαρὰ ἐνδεδυμένος ἱμάτια, ἀλλὰ τῷ γάμῳ κατάλληλον λαβὲ στολήν.
thought_title: Grace dispels the mind's darkness; Christ becomes all things to the baptized
orientation: Chrysostom is addressing the catechumens, continuing his explanation of how baptism's grace changes the soul's perception and then turning to exhortation about how they must now live.
pass_a_gloss: For when the grace comes and drives away the darkness from the mind, we learn the exact truth of things, and the things that were formerly fearful become contemptible to us. For we no longer fear death, having learned exactly from this sacred initiation, that death is not death, but sleep and a temporary slumber; nor poverty, nor sickness, nor any other of such things, knowing that we are journeying toward a better life, pure and incorruptible, and freed from every such irregularity. 2. Let us therefore no longer remain gaping at the things of this life, nor at the luxury of the table, nor at the costliness of garments; for you have the greatest garment, you have a spiritual table, you have the glory above, and Christ becomes all things to you, both table, and garment, and house, and head, and root. For as many of you as were baptized into Christ, you put on Christ; behold how he has become a garment to you. Do you wish to learn how he also becomes a table to you? The one who eats me, he says, just as I live because of the Father, that one also will live because of me. And that he also becomes a house to you: The one who eats my flesh remains in me, and I in him; and that he is a root, again he says: I am the vine, you are the branches; and that he is brother, and friend, and bridegroom: No longer do I call you servants; for you are my friends. And Paul again: I betrothed you to one husband, to present a pure virgin to Christ; and again: So that he might be firstborn among many brothers. And we become not only his brothers, but also children; For behold, he says, I and the children whom God has given me; and not this only, but also his members, and his body. For as if the things said were not sufficient to show the love and the goodwill which he shows toward us, he also set another thing greater and nearer than these, calling himself our head. Knowing all these things, beloved, repay your benefactor with the best conduct, and having considered the greatness of the sacrifice, adorn the members of your body. Consider what you receive in your hand, and never endure to strike anyone, nor disgrace the hand honored with so great a gift by the sin of a blow; consider what you receive in your hand, and keep it pure from greed and all robbery. Reckon that you receive not only with the hand, but you also bring it to the mouth, and keep the tongue pure from shameful and insolent words, from blasphemy, from perjury, and from all the other such things. For it is destructive to divert the tongue that serves such most awesome sacred rites, and has been dyed red with such blood, and has become golden, to abuse and insults and coarse jesting. Respect the honor with which God honored it, and do not bring it down to the cheapness of sin; but having considered again, that after the hand and the tongue the heart receives that awesome sacred rite, never stitch up deceit against your neighbor, but keep your mind pure from all wickedness; thus you will be able to secure also your eyes and your hearing. For how is it not absurd, after that mystical voice, the one borne from the heavens, I mean the one from the Cherubim, to defile the hearing with pornographic songs and broken melodies? And how is it not worthy of the utmost punishment, with the eyes with which you see the secret and awesome sacred rites, with these to look at prostitutes, and to commit adultery in the mind? You have been called to a wedding, beloved; do not enter wearing filthy garments, but take a garment suitable for the wedding.

choices.why: Fixed glossary term for baptism as complete re-creation.
Fixed glossary term for baptism as initiation into the sacred mysteries.
Fixed glossary term for the sacred rites, especially baptism and the Eucharist.
Fixed glossary term for false swearing.
μείνωμεν is 'let us remain/stay,' not 'stand'; κεχηνότες is 'gaping' as a state of open-mouthed fixation.
The verb ῥάπτω means to sew or stitch; the metaphor is of fabricating or devising deceit.

pass_b_english: For when grace comes and drives the darkness from the mind, we learn the truth about things, and what once terrified us becomes contemptible. We no longer fear death, because we have learned precisely from this sacred initiation that death is not death, but sleep and a temporary slumber. We do not fear poverty, or sickness, or anything else of that kind, because we know that we are traveling toward a better life, pure and incorruptible, free from every such irregularity.

Let us no longer remain gaping at the things of this life, nor at the luxury of the table, nor at the extravagance of clothing. For you have the greatest garment, you have a spiritual table, you have the glory from above, and Christ becomes everything for you: table, garment, house, head, and root. “For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3:27). See how he has become your garment. Do you want to learn how he also becomes your table? “Whoever eats me,” he says, “as I live because of the Father, so he also will live because of me” (John 6:57). And that he becomes your house: “Whoever eats my flesh remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:56). And that he is the root, he says again: “I am the vine, you are the branches” (John 15:5). And that he is brother, and friend, and bridegroom: “No longer do I call you servants, for you are my friends” (John 15:15). And Paul again: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2). And again: “That he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8:29). And we become not only his brothers, but also his children: “Behold,” he says, “I and the children whom God has given me” (Isaiah 8:18). And not only this, but also his members, and his body. For as if the things already said were not enough to show the love and goodwill he displays toward us, he added something greater and closer than all these, calling himself our head.

Knowing all these things, beloved, repay your benefactor with the best way of life, and when you consider the greatness of the sacrifice, adorn the members of your body. Consider what you receive in your hand, and never endure to strike anyone, nor disgrace the hand honored with so great a gift by the sin of a blow. Consider what you receive in your hand, and keep it pure from greed and all robbery. Reckon that you do not receive it only with your hand, but you also bring it to your mouth, and keep your tongue pure from shameful and abusive words, from blasphemy, from perjury, and from all other such things. For it is destructive to turn a tongue that serves such awe-inspiring sacred rites, that has been dyed red with such blood and become a golden sword, to use it for insults, abuse, and coarse jesting. Respect the honor with which God has honored it, and do not drag it down into the cheapness of sin. But consider again that after the hand and the tongue, the heart receives that awe-inspiring mystery, and never stitch up deceit against your neighbor, but keep your mind pure from all wickedness. In this way you will also be able to guard your eyes and your hearing. For how is it not absurd, after that mystical voice that comes from heaven—I mean the voice of the Cherubim—to defile your hearing with pornographic songs and effeminate melodies? And how is it not worthy of the utmost punishment, with the eyes with which you see the ineffable and awe-inspiring sacred rites, to look at prostitutes with those same eyes and commit adultery in your mind? You have been invited to a wedding, beloved. Do not enter wearing filthy clothes, but take a garment suited to the wedding.
notes: The source text contains 'γλῶτ49.234 ταν' which appears to be OCR damage or a page/line number inserted into the word γλῶτταν; the gloss treats it as γλῶτταν (tongue).

problems.quote: that has been dyed red with such blood and become golden, into a sword for insults
problems.source_quote: καὶ αἵματι φοινιχθεῖσαν τοιοῦτῳ, καὶ χρυσῆν γενομένην μάχαιραν, ἐπὶ λοιδορίας
problems.why: Source says the tongue became a golden sword; English makes 'sword' the thing it is turned into, losing that the tongue itself became a golden sword.
problems.fix: that has been dyed red with such blood and become a golden sword, to use it for insults
problems.ruling: Greek: tongue 'became a golden sword' (χρυσῆν γενομένην μάχαιραν); English makes 'sword' the object turned into, not what tongue became.

problems.why: κατακεκλασμένοις means 'effeminate' or 'languishing,' not 'broken.' The English misrepresents the moral critique of decadent music.
problems.ruling: κατακεκλασμένοις μέλεσι means 'languishing/effeminate melodies,' not 'broken'; moral critique is lost.

edits.old: that has been dyed red with such blood and become golden, into a sword for insults
edits.new: that has been dyed red with such blood and become a golden sword, to use it for insults

fixed: Corrected: the tongue itself became a golden sword, not that it was turned into a sword for insults.
Corrected: κατακεκλασμένοις means effeminate or languishing, not broken.

problems.quote: as I live because of the Father, so he also will live because of me
problems.source_quote: ὥσπερ ἐγὼ ζῶ διὰ τὸν Πατέρα, κἀκεῖνος ζήσεται δι' ἐμέ
problems.why: English reverses the living relationship: source says 'as I live because of the Father, so he will live because of me' (correct), but 'so he also will live' makes it sound like the believer's living is parallel to Christ's, when it's 'that one will live'—the same pattern of dependent life.
problems.fix: as I live because of the Father, so that one will live because of me

edits.old: as I live because of the Father, so he also will live because of me
edits.new: as I live because of the Father, so that one will live because of me

fixed: Changed 'so he also will live' to 'so that one will live' to match the source's demonstrative κἀκεῖνος, which points to the eater rather than paralleling the believer with Christ.

problems.quote: as I live because of the Father, so that one will live because of me
problems.source_quote: ὁ τρώγων με, φησὶν, ὥσπερ ἐγὼ ζῶ διὰ τὸν Πατέρα, κἀκεῖνος ζήσεται δι' ἐμέ
problems.why: Wrong subject: 'that one' refers to the eater, but 'κἀκεῖνος' means 'and he' i.e. 'so he will live because of me'—the eater lives, not Christ.
problems.fix: 'Whoever eats me,' he says, 'just as I live because of the Father, so also will that one live because of me'
problems.ruling: 'κἀκεῖνος' = 'and he' (the eater), not 'that one'; 'so he will live' is correct, not 'so that one will live'

edits.old: as I live because of the Father, so that one will live because of me
edits.new: as I live because of the Father, so he also will live because of me

fixed: The English 'so that one will live because of me' is ambiguous and could be read as Christ living because of the eater, but the source 'κἀκεῖνος ζήσεται δι' ἐμέ' clearly means the eater will live because of Christ. The earlier edit to 'so he also will live because of me' is correct and should be restored.

last_rejected.why: Source says the voice comes FROM the Cherubim, not that it IS the voice of the Cherubim.
last_rejected.fix: I mean the one from the Cherubim
last_rejected.ruling: τὴν ἐκ τῶν Χερουβὶμ λέγω = 'the one from the Cherubim, I mean' — English paraphrase is accurate.

last_rejected.why: κατακεκλασμένοις means 'broken, languishing, voluptuous' not 'effeminate'; misrepresents the sensual/languid character of the music.
last_rejected.ruling: κατακεκλασμένοις can mean 'bent, languishing'; 'effeminate' captures the moralizing sense adequately.

last_rejected.why: πορνικοῖς means 'licentious, fornicating, whorish'—songs that lead to or celebrate sexual immorality, not modern 'pornographic'.
last_rejected.fix: licentious songs or songs of fornication
last_rejected.ruling: πορνικοῖς relates to πορνεία/porneia; 'pornographic' conveys sexual immorality adequately for modern readers.

last_rejected.why: εὐτραπελία is witty, clever, urbane mockery/banter, not 'coarse'; the danger is refined, clever ridicule, not roughness.
last_rejected.ruling: εὐτραπελία ranges from wit to coarse jesting; 'coarse jesting' is a standard rendering in patristic moral contexts.

last_rejected.source_quote: μὴ ῥάψῃς ποτὲ κατὰ τοῦ πλησίον δόλον
last_rejected.why: ῥάψῃς is 'sew, weave, contrive'—'stitch up' suggests framing someone; better 'weave' or 'contrive' deceit.
last_rejected.ruling: ῥάψῃς + δόλον literally means 'sew deceit'; 'stitch up deceit' is a legitimate English rendering, not necessarily 'framing'.
